clue.text: Reader's expectation from a good writer

definitions.text: Reader's expectation from a good writer

parts.words: Reader's expectation from a good writer
parts.note: a 'good writer' sounds like a skilled author, but here it means someone with neat handwriting, whose script a reader expects to be able to make out

explanation.surface: What a book lover hopes for from a talented author.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests literary quality; the real sense is penmanship, so what the reader expects is simply clear, decipherable handwriting.
explanation.definitionFit: Clear handwriting has the quality of being readable, which is what a reader hopes a careful penman will supply.

clue.text: They might put up travelling craftsmen

definitions.text: They might put up travelling craftsmen

parts.words: They might put up travelling craftsmen
parts.note: putting up sounds like giving lodging to itinerant artisans, but it means raising boats and their crews on a canal

explanation.surface: Inns that might accommodate wandering artisans.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'craftsmen' as the people on craft (boats): canal gates raise vessels travelling up a waterway.
explanation.definitionFit: Canal chambers with gates raise or lower boats between water levels.

clue.text: Perhaps they left by local 'time

parts.note: recalls a pub landlord's closing call 'Time, ... please', after which the drinkers at the local leave

explanation.surface: Travellers who set off according to the local clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'local' is a British pub, and 'time' is the landlord's call at closing; the customers addressed in that call are the ones leaving.
explanation.definitionFit: The polite term for men is the word in the traditional closing-time call to drinkers.

clue.text: Alloy suitable for trident?

parts.note: the figure personifying Britain carries a trident, so an alloy named after her would suit it

explanation.surface: Asking which metal would best make a three-pronged spear.
explanation.walkthrough: Britannia, the female emblem of Britain, is shown holding a trident; a tin-based alloy bears her name.
explanation.definitionFit: A silvery tin alloy with antimony and copper, used for tableware, is named after the national figure of Britain.

clue.text: Pull fish up on the sheltered side

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the pieces are read from bottom to top

parts.note: draw means pull
an eel is a fish

explanation.surface: Hauling a fish aboard on the side out of the wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DRAWEEL, the pull and the fish together, so it reads from the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The side away from the wind is the sheltered side on a ship.

clue.text: Bad drivers given a lift at Ascot?

definitions.text: Bad drivers given a lift at Ascot?

parts.words: Bad drivers given a lift at Ascot?
parts.note: golfers who hit the ball on its upper half make poor drives; the same word names tall silk hats raised in greeting at the Ascot races

explanation.surface: Poor motorists offered a ride at the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a famous English racecourse where formal top hats are worn; in golf, topping the ball is a fault.
explanation.definitionFit: Silk hats raised at Ascot share a name with golfers who top their drives.

clue.text: Some nice Pickwickian poem?

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A question about whether a pleasant Dickensian figure deserves verse.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a long narrative poem about heroic deeds, such as the Iliad.

clue.text: Part in silence, say

indicators.note: say means as spoken, so the word for silence is heard rather than spelt

parts.note: peace means silence or quiet

explanation.surface: A role played without speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A piece is a portion or fragment of something.

clue.text: Vessel is another going outside a river

indicators.note: going outside means the container word is wrapped round the other pieces

parts.note: a can is a vessel, a container
the Tamar is a river between Devon and Cornwall

explanation.surface: One ship travels out of a river mouth after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' is a can for the wordplay, and 'another' is the definition: another kind of vessel, a boat. The River Tamar divides Devon from Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: A twin-hulled boat is one more type of seagoing craft, so it is a further example of a vessel.

clue.text: Event in which athlete should not be out of 'bounds?

definitions.text: Event in which athlete should not be out of 'bounds?

parts.words: Event in which athlete should not be out of 'bounds?
parts.note: out of bounds suggests straying off the field, but bounds are leaps; the competitor in this jumping event must not run short of springs

explanation.surface: A sports event where competitors must stay inside the marked area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bounds' looks like boundaries; it means leaps, and this athletics event is a sequence of three of them (the old name for the triple jump).
explanation.definitionFit: The old name for the triple jump describes its three phases of leaping.

clue.text: Frank East wrote this satire

parts.note: frank means candid, open and honest

explanation.surface: A man called Frank East is credited with writing a satirical work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank East' reads as a person's name; it is two pieces. The satire is Voltaire's, and 'wrote this' just links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Voltaire's Candide is a famous satirical novel mocking blind optimism.

clue.text: Guard for sleuth, they say — a sort of square

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
'tec is a colloquial clipping of detective, so 'they say' marks it as slang
a T-square is a draughtsman's tool, so T is a kind of square

explanation.surface: A security guard is recommended for a detective who is rather old-fashioned.
explanation.definitionFit: To guard something is to shield or keep it safe from harm.

clue.text: Territory might be Roman? Not right

definitions.text: Territory might be Roman? Not right

parts.words: Territory might be Roman? Not right
parts.note: the word Roman without its R (right) leaves the name of a Gulf state ruled by a sultan, so the clue offers that country as an example of this kind of territory

explanation.surface: Someone guesses a land might have been part of the Roman Empire and is told they are wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R (right) from ROMAN to get OMAN; the answer is the kind of territory Oman is, so this is a definition by example rather than letter-building.
explanation.definitionFit: Oman is ruled by a sultan, so it is a state of the type governed by such a monarch.

clue.text: Riotous mates go for .old captain

indicators.note: riotous means wild and disorderly, so the letters of the next word run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: Unruly shipmates set off in search of their former skipper.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of MATES gives the word an old steamship captain would use for moving ahead under power.
explanation.definitionFit: To an old ship's captain, the vapour-driven engine is what made a vessel move, so the word meant to proceed.

clue.text: Novel French type

definitions.meaning: the French word for a novel
the ordinary upright typeface, as opposed to italic

explanation.surface: A new style of French lettering.
explanation.definitionFit: In French a novel is called by this word, and in printing it names plain upright lettering rather than italics.

clue.text: Free, but a pound collected — could be disproved

indicators.note: collected means gathered and assembled afresh, so the letters are put together in a new order

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A claim that something free but costing a pound could be shown false.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be shown false is open to disproof.

clue.text: Underworld boss meets farmer — Scotchman, perhaps?

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god who rules the underworld
a tiller is one who tills, or cultivates, the land

explanation.surface: A gangster teams up with a farmer, and the result might be a Scotsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underworld boss' suggests a gangster but is the god Dis. 'Scotchman' is a whisky-maker: one who makes Scotch.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of Scotch whisky is the producer who runs the still, so 'Scotchman' is a playful description of one.

clue.text: I love the answer to this Richard's clue

definitions.text: I love the answer to this Richard's clue

parts.words: I love the answer to this Richard's clue
parts.note: suggests the setter loves the solution, but refers to King Richard I's epithet, the big cat's courage, as the 'clue' to him

explanation.surface: Someone named Richard writes a crossword clue and the setter adores its solution.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard I of England was called Coeur de Lion; the answer is the epithet that identifies him, and 'heart' in it plays on 'love'.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard I's nickname means a person of great courage, the big cat's spirit.

clue.text: Excellent description of a dancer's toe?

definitions.meaning: from Milton's line about tripping it on the light ... toe, a phrase used of dancing

explanation.surface: A glowing review of a ballet dancer's footwork.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's 'L'Allegro' has 'trip it as you go, On the light fantastic toe', and 'trip the light fantastic' became a phrase for dancing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means marvellous, and Milton applied it to the dancing toe in a famous line.

clue.text: Barker appears to blunder into row

indicators.note: into means the blunder word is placed inside the row word

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats
err means blunder, make a mistake

explanation.surface: A loud man seems to stumble into an argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' looks like a quarrel; it is a line, a tier of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: A barker is a dog, and this breed is a small, noisy dog.

clue.text: Food for strikers going round?

definitions.meaning: the dishes of a meal, served one after another
golfers, who strike balls, go round these

explanation.surface: Supplies brought to workers on a picket line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strikers' suggests workers on strike; they are golfers striking balls.
explanation.definitionFit: A meal is served in stages of dishes, and golfers play round grounds known by the same word.

clue.text: Deck party in a Navy setting

indicators.note: a setting holds a jewel, so A and the Navy letters form a mount around the party

parts.note: RN is the abbreviation for the Royal Navy
a do is an informal word for a party

explanation.surface: A party is held aboard a naval ship, with the deck as its venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' is a verb here, to decorate, not a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck something is to decorate or embellish it.

clue.text: Numbers to note in future, perhaps

parts.note: tens are numbers
E is a musical note

explanation.surface: Someone forecasts what figures will matter in years to come.
explanation.definitionFit: The future is one grammatical form showing when an action happens, alongside past and present.

clue.text: Music one found in part of Bible

indicators.note: found in means one is placed inside the part of the Bible

parts.note: NT is the abbreviation for the New Testament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A single song discovered in a section of scripture.
explanation.definitionFit: A composition for nine performers is a piece of music.

clue.text: Drive, perhaps, to get ammunition

definitions.meaning: a drive is one stroke taken in a round of golf or a cricket innings
solid cannonballs fired from old guns

explanation.surface: A golf stroke made to win some ammunition.
explanation.definitionFit: A drive is a shot in a round, and the same phrase names the spherical solid projectiles fired from cannons.

clue.text: Might be ground for great frustration

definitions.text: Might be ground for great frustration

parts.words: Might be ground for great frustration
parts.note: ground looks like a reason or basis, but it is the past participle of grind: people grind these when frustrated

explanation.surface: A possible cause of serious annoyance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ground' is not 'grounds' but grind's past form: people grind or gnash these in frustration.
explanation.definitionFit: The things in the mouth used for chewing are gnashed in anger.

clue.text: An Asian or Scottish mount one convict backed

parts.note: ben is the Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis

indicators.note: backed says the pair of words one and convict are read in reverse

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
lag is slang for a convict, as in old lag

explanation.surface: Someone from Asia, or a Scottish mountain climbed by a convict on the run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' turns ILAG to GALI after BEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Bengal, in India and Bangladesh, is a person from Asia.

clue.text: Assumed by priest to be sensible about striking

indicators.note: about means around, so the word for sensible wraps the word for striking

parts.note: sane means sensible, of sound mind
out means on strike, as in workers being out

explanation.surface: A clergyman wants to seem reasonable about an industrial dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assumed' means put on, as of a garment, not taken for granted.
explanation.definitionFit: A cassock is put on by a Catholic priest, and to assume clothing is to don it.

clue.text: Artist Elizabeth beheaded

indicators.note: beheaded means the first letter of the name is cut off

parts.note: Betty is a pet form of the name Elizabeth

explanation.surface: A historical report that an artist called Elizabeth lost her head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artist Elizabeth' reads as one person; the painter is William Etty, a 19th-century English artist known for nudes.
explanation.definitionFit: William Etty was an English painter of the early Victorian era.

clue.text: Ill-natured person presents monument' to beauty-spot

parts.note: a cross, such as a market cross, can be a memorial monument
a patch was a small piece of black silk worn on the face as a beauty spot

explanation.surface: A grumpy person gives a beauty spot to a monument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beauty-spot' sounds like a scenic place; it is the fashionable face patch of the 17th and 18th centuries.
explanation.definitionFit: A grumpy, bad-tempered person is a familiar sense of the compound.
